reason: The cited evidence (E1-E4) supports the creation of a nanoporous structure with a surface oxide layer via dealloying a multi-principal-element alloy and its high activity/stability in electrocatalysis. However, the hypothesis extrapolates these findings to automotive exhaust catalysis without any cited evidence for CO/hydrocarbon oxidation, resistance to H2O/NO poisoning, or durability under vehicle-aging conditions. The key premise that these properties will translate to the automotive exhaust environment is entirely unsupported by the provided passages.
premises: Dealloying a multi-principal-element alloy can create a nanoporous structure with a surface oxide layer.
This nanoporous structure with surface oxide can exhibit high catalytic activity and stability.
The surface oxide layer is enriched in certain elements (e.g., Nb and O) while deficient in others.
The multi-principal-element composition provides thermal stability and reduces platinum-group-metal use.
The enhanced activity and stability observed in electrocatalysis will translate to automotive exhaust catalysis under transient, low-temperature, and poisoning conditions.
